the PCAIs inhibit angiogenesis by disrupting the GTPase cycle of monomeric Ras and Rab proteins.
polyisoprenated cysteinylamide inhibitors block angiogenesis in human umbilical vascular endothelial cells, chick embryo, and zebrafishes.
the polyisopreylated cysteinly amide inhibitors inhibit angiogenesis in HUVEC cells and in chick embryos and zebrafishes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing safer and effective angiogenesis inhibitors.
developing novel therapeutics that target the aberrant G-protein signaling in cancers.
the development of small molecules that inhibit angiogenesis and thereby tumor growth.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the antiangiogenic effects observed in HUVEC and in the CAM and zebraﬁsh models were due to the polyisoprene moiety and not the cysteine amide moiety.
polyisoprenoid moiety of the PCAIs is essential to block the angiogenic effects of the PCAIs.
the antiangiogenic effects are independent of the cell death and are dependent on the poly-isoprenylated moiety.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the antiangiogenic properties of PCAIs are due to the polyisoprene moiety, and the antiangiogenic effects are independent of their effects on Ras.
the PCAIs are effective antiangiogenic agents that are independent of the RTKs signaling and can be developed into therapeutics for cancer and retinal neorvascularization.
the PCAIs are effective antiangiogenic compounds that block angiogenesis in HUVEC tube formation, CAM and zebrafish models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
polyisoprenated small G-protein signaling is essential for angiogenesis and the PCAIs are effective inhibitors of angiogenesis.
the PCAIs are effective antiangiogenic agents that block the monomeric Ras signaling.
the PCAIs can be developed into therapeutics that can block angiogenesis without affecting the other physiological functions of polyisoprylated proteins.
